title: The Remainder Sign Flips the Bound Direction
content:
The key algebraic fact is that when dividing x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n) by (1+x²), the remainder (a constant) alternates in sign with n:

- n=1: remainder = (1-i)^4 = -4 → integral = r - π > 0 → π < r (upper bound)
- n=2: remainder = (1-i)^8 = 16 → integral = 4π - r > 0 → π > r/4 (lower bound)
- n=3: remainder = (1-i)^12 = -64 → integral = r - 16π > 0 → π < r/16 (upper bound)

This alternating pattern means successive Dalzell integrals give alternating upper/lower bounds, converging to π from both sides.

The remainder is computed by evaluating x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n) at the root of (1+x²), i.e., at x = i (the imaginary unit): i^(4n) = 1 and (1-i)^(4n) depends on n.
mathContext: The polynomial remainder theorem: when P(x) = (x²+1)Q(x) + (ax+b), evaluating at x=i gives P(i) = ai + b. For x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n), the value at x=i is i^(4n)(1-i)^(4n) = (1-i)^(4n). Since (1-i)^4 = -4, we get the pattern: n=1 → -4, n=2 → 16, n=3 → -64, n=4 → 256. The imaginary part is always 0 (the polynomial has real coefficients), so the remainder is a real constant.
prerequisites: complex number evaluation of real polynomials

title: Term-by-Term HasDerivAt Chain for Degree-14 Antiderivative
content:
The antiderivative F₂ has 12 terms (a degree-14 polynomial plus 16·arctan). The proof constructs F₂' = dalzell2Decomposed via a chain of 11 HasDerivAt compositions:

```lean
have hcomb := ((((((((((h15.sub h14).add h13).sub h12).add h11)
  .sub h10).sub h9).add h7).sub h5).add h3).sub h1).add ha
```

This follows the same pattern as the parent proof's 5-term chain, just extended. Each term's derivative is proved using `hasDerivAt_pow`, `.const_mul`, `.div_const`, and `hasDerivAt_arctan`, with `convert ... using 1; push_cast; ring` to normalize the derivative value.

The chain works because Lean's `HasDerivAt.sub` and `HasDerivAt.add` compose left-associatively, matching the left-associative parsing of arithmetic expressions in Lean.
mathContext: The antiderivative F₂(x) = x¹⁵/15 - 4x¹⁴/7 + 27x¹³/13 - 4x¹² + 43x¹¹/11 - 4x¹⁰/5 - 5x⁹/3 + 16x⁷/7 - 16x⁵/5 + 16x³/3 - 16x + 16·arctan(x). Note x⁷ and x⁵ and x³ terms come from integrating the even-only polynomial Q (which has no odd-degree terms except via the polynomial itself).

title: FTC via F₂(1) - F₂(0): Exact Rational + π Computation
content:
The integral value 4π - 188684/15015 comes from:

  F₂(1) - F₂(0) = (1/15 - 4/7 + 27/13 - 4 + 43/11 - 4/5 - 5/3 + 16/7 - 16/5 + 16/3 - 16 + 4π) - 0

The rational sum over LCM(15,7,13,11,3) = 15015:
  (1001 + 25740 + 31185 - 60060 + 58695 - 12012 - 25025 + 34320 - 48048 + 80080 - 240240) / 15015
  = -188684 / 15015

The arctan term: 16·arctan(1) = 16·(π/4) = 4π (by `arctan_one`).

In Lean: after `rw [arctan_one]`, the `ring` tactic verifies F₂(1) = 4π - 188684/15015 by computing the rational arithmetic automatically.
mathContext: The fraction -188684/15015 is in lowest terms (GCD = 1). The bound it gives: π > 47171/15015 ≈ 3.14156 vs π ≈ 3.14159. The integral itself is approximately 4π - 188684/15015 ≈ 4×3.14159 - 12.56637 ≈ 0.0000023, a tiny positive number confirming the integrand is very small.

title: π > 47171/15015: Lower Bound from Integral Positivity
content:
The lower bound proof follows directly from two facts:
1. ∫₀¹ x⁸(1-x)⁸/(1+x²) dx = 4π - 188684/15015 (integral identity)
2. ∫₀¹ x⁸(1-x)⁸/(1+x²) dx > 0 (integrand is positive on (0,1))

Combining: 4π - 188684/15015 > 0 → π > 188684/60060 = 47171/15015.

The `linarith` tactic closes this after establishing the two facts. The positivity comes from `integral_pos`, which requires:
- ContinuousOn on [0,1]
- Nonneg everywhere on [0,1]
- Strictly positive at some interior point (x=1/2 is the witness)

This is the opposite direction from the parent proof's conclusion π < 22/7, which used the same integral_pos approach but with the n=1 integral equaling 22/7 - π > 0.
mathContext: The key contrast with n=1: the n=1 integral = 22/7 - π > 0 gives an UPPER bound (22/7 > π). The n=2 integral = 4π - 188684/15015 > 0 gives a LOWER bound (π > 47171/15015). The remainder's sign flips the direction of the bound.

title: Two-Sided Rational Sandwich: 47171/15015 < π < 22/7
content:
pi_rational_sandwich packages the two bounds into a conjunction:

  47171/15015 < π   (n=2 lower bound, this file)
  π < 22/7           (n=1 upper bound, from parent AreaOfCircleOQ03OQ02OQ02)

Numerically: 3.14156... < π < 3.14286...

This gives π correct to 4 decimal places (π = 3.1415...) using only rational approximations. The Dalzell method provides a purely analytic (integration-based) proof that π is approximately 3.14159 without computing more than two specific rational approximations.

The convergence pattern for higher n:
- n=1: π < 22/7 ≈ 3.14286 (error ≈ 0.00126)
- n=2: π > 47171/15015 ≈ 3.14156 (error ≈ 0.00003)
- n=3: π < q₃ (tighter upper bound)
- n=4: π > q₄ (tighter lower bound)

The bounds converge to π since ∫₀¹ x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n)/(1+x²) dx → 0.
mathContext: Archimedes' method (inscribed/circumscribed polygons) gave 223/71 < π < 22/7. This Dalzell method gives a comparable lower bound via integration theory, with the same upper bound 22/7 from Dalzell n=1. The lower bound 47171/15015 ≈ 3.14156 is weaker than Archimedes' 223/71 ≈ 3.14085... wait, 223/71 ≈ 3.14085, which is actually less accurate. The Dalzell lower bound 47171/15015 is much tighter.

title: The Dalzell Sequence: Alternating Upper/Lower Bounds on π
content:
The Dalzell integral sequence Iₙ = ∫₀¹ x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n)/(1+x²) dx satisfies:

1. Iₙ > 0 for all n (integrand is nonneg and strictly positive somewhere)
2. Iₙ → 0 as n → ∞ (since x^(4n)(1-x)^(4n) → 0 pointwise)
3. Iₙ = aₙ·π - bₙ for explicit rationals aₙ, bₙ (from polynomial long division)

From (1) and (3): aₙ·π > bₙ (if aₙ > 0) or aₙ·π < bₙ (if aₙ < 0).

For n=1: a₁ = -1 (from remainder -4 → ∫16/(1+x²) = -arctan terms = -π), I₁ = 22/7 - π → π < 22/7
For n=2: a₂ = 4 (from remainder +16 → 4π term), I₂ = 4π - 188684/15015 → π > 47171/15015

From (2): bₙ/aₙ → π, giving increasingly precise rational approximations.

This file formally verifies the n=2 case, answering the open question from the parent proof affirmatively.
mathContext: The sequence (bₙ/aₙ) converges to π at rate O(1/16^n) approximately (since max{x^4(1-x)^4} = (1/4)^4·(1/4)^4/(5/4) = (1/4)^8/(5/4), and scaling by n). This is slow convergence compared to e.g. the Gauss-Legendre algorithm, but the proof is elementary and elegant.
